The '''2nd Academy Awards''', presented by the [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] (AMPAS) on April 3, 1930, at an awards banquet in the Cocoanut Grove of the [[Ambassador Hotel (Los Angeles)|Ambassador Hotel]] in [[Los Angeles]], honored the best films released between August 1, 1928, and July 31, 1929.<ref name=LATimes>{{cite news |title=Academy Awards Acting Honors to Mary Pickford as 'Coquette' and Warner Baxter in 'Old Arizona' |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-2d-aas-winners-193/134425356/ |access-date=January 18, 2026 |work=The Los Angeles Times |date=April 4, 1930 |pages=32}}</ref> This was the first Academy Awards ceremony broadcast on radio, by local station [[KNX (AM)|KNX]], Los Angeles.<ref name="Dunning">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EwtRbXNca0oC&dq=%22The+Academy+Awards+Show%22&pg=PA4 |last=Dunning| first=John| author-link=John Dunning (detective fiction author) | title=On the Air: The Encyclopedia of Old-Time Radio| date=1998| publisher=Oxford University Press| location=New York, NY| isbn=978-0-19-507678-3| pages=4–5 | edition=Revised| access-date=2019-09-10}} </ref><ref name="Oscars '28-29 Notes">{{cite book |last1=Wallechinsky |first1=David |last2=Wallace |first2=Irving |date=1975 |title=The People's Almanac |url=https://archive.org/details/peoplesalmanac00wall/page/830/mode/2up |location=Garden City, New York |publisher=Doubleday & Company, Inc. |page=831 |isbn=0-385-04060-1}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Academy Making Awards Tonight |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/los-angeles-evening-citizen-news-academy/169591808/ |access-date=January 15, 2026 |work=Los Angeles Evening Citizen News |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=April 3, 1930 |page=2}}</ref> Over 300 attended the event, which included Academy members and guests.<ref name=LATimes/>

The second ceremony included a number of changes from the first: most importantly, it was the first presentation for which the winners were not announced in advance, and the number of award categories was reduced from twelve to seven. It is unique in that there were never any official nominees; instead, AMPAS conducted further research and came up with a list of unofficial or de facto nominees using records of the films that the judges had given their opinions on. [[Chester Morris]] was the first nominee for [[Academy Award for Best Actor|Best Actor]] to be born in the 20th century.

[[Mary Pickford]], a founding member of AMPAS and married to its first president,<ref name="Oscars '28-29 Notes"/> lobbied to be considered for the [[Academy Award for Best Actress|Best Actress]] award, inviting the judges over for tea at her home,<ref>{{cite book |last=Whitfield |first=Eileen |author-link=Eileen Whitfield |title=Pickford: The Woman Who Made Hollywood |year=1997 |publisher=University Press of Kentucky |location=Lexington, Ky. |isbn=978-0-8131-2045-4 |oclc=37465308|page=263|title-link=Pickford: The Woman Who Made Hollywood }}</ref> while other actresses being considered for the same award were not made aware of their status.<ref>{{cite news|title=The Actress and the Four-Letter Cliche|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|location=London|date=April 28, 1972|page=13|last=White|first=Michael|author-link=Michael White (journalist)|quote=As the elder sister in ''Broadway Melody'' she got an Oscar nomination, which in all honesty she doesn't recall at all. 'So many people have said it that it must be true.'}}</ref>

[[Jeanne Eagels]] became the first and, to date, only actress to be posthumously nominated for Best Actress, for ''[[The Letter (1929 film)|The Letter]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last=O'Connor |first=Clint |title=James Dean, Spencer Tracy among posthumous Oscar nods|publisher=[[The Plain Dealer]]|date=July 13, 2008|url=http://www.cleveland.com/movies/index.ssf/2008/07/james_dean_spencer_tracy_among.html|accessdate=February 23, 2014|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20121014023959/http://www.cleveland.com/movies/index.ssf/2008/07/james_dean_spencer_tracy_among.html|archivedate=October 14, 2012}}</ref> ''[[The Divine Lady]]'' became the last film to win Best Director without receiving a Best Picture nomination.

This is the only year in which no film won more than one Oscar. ''[[The Broadway Melody]]'' became the second of seven films to win Best Picture without a writing nomination (preceded by ''[[Wings (1927 film)|Wings]]'', and followed by ''[[Grand Hotel (1932 film)|Grand Hotel]]'', ''[[Cavalcade (1933 film)|Cavalcade]]'', ''[[Hamlet (1948 film)|Hamlet]]'', ''[[The Sound of Music (film)|The Sound of Music]]'', and ''[[Titanic (1997 film)|Titanic]]''), and the first of three to win Best Picture and nothing else (followed by ''Grand Hotel'' and ''[[Mutiny on the Bounty (1935 film)|Mutiny on the Bounty]]'').

== Multiple nominations and awards ==
''[[In Old Arizona]]'' and ''[[The Patriot (1928 film)|The Patriot]]'', with five nominations each, tied the record for the film receiving the most Academy Award nominations. This record was set by ''[[7th Heaven (1927 film)|7th Heaven]]'' at the [[1st Academy Awards]] (1927{{ndash}}1928). One year later, at the [[3rd Academy Awards]] (1929{{ndash}}1930), the record was broken by ''[[The Love Parade]]'', which garnered six nominations. The record for the film receiving the most Academy Award nominations {{ndash}} with sixteen nominations {{ndash}} is held by ''[[Sinners (2025 film)|Sinners]]'' (2025).<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/awards/story/2026-01-22/sinners-record-most-oscar-nominations-2026 |title=‘Sinners’ sweeps Oscar nominations, breaking record with 16 |last=Rottenberg |first=Josh |work=The Los Angeles Times |date=January 22, 2026 |access-date=January 23, 2026}}</ref> The previous record of fourteen nominations was held by ''[[All About Eve]]'' (1950), ''[[Titanic (1997 film)|Titanic]]'' (1997), and ''[[La La Land (film)|La La Land]]'' (2016).<!-- Comment: For the template formula to calculate correctly, the "year of the film" must be INCREASED by ONE. So, for a 1950 film, enter 1951 into the template. -->

== Changes to Academy Awards ==

Beginning with the 2nd Academy Awards (1928{{ndash}}1929), the following changes were made by [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences|AMPAS]].

* Award categories were reduced from twelve to seven:
** The awards for Best Director (Comedy Picture) and Best Director (Dramatic Picture) were merged into a single Best Director award.
** The awards for Best Writing (Adaptation) and Best Writing (Original Story) were merged into a single Best Writing award (these would be split again for the [[4th Academy Awards|4th Awards]]).
** The awards for Best Engineering Effects, Best Unique and Artistic Production, and Best Writing (Title Writing) were discontinued.
